items.front: Angle between clock hands at H:M?
items.back: Angle = |30H − 5.5M| degrees (take value ≤180°). Minute hand gains 5.5°/min on the hour hand.

items.front: In 12 hours, how often do hands coincide / oppose / make right angles?
items.back: Coincide 11, opposite 11, right angles 22 (double for 24 h → 22, 22, 44). Coincide every 65 5/11 min.
items.examPoint: Clock — hands opposite / in a straight line (180°)

items.front: When do hands coincide / make 90° between hour H and H+1?
items.back: Solve 30H = 5.5M (overlap at 60H/11 min) or |30H−5.5M| = 90. Hands overlap once every 720/11 min.
items.examPoint: Clock — time when the hands coincide (65 5/11 min gap)

items.front: Faulty clock: total error, and does it read early or late?
items.back: Total error = per-hour error × hours elapsed. Losing clock reads EARLIER; gaining clock reads LATER.
items.examPoint: Clock — faulty clock gaining or losing time

items.front: Mirror image of a clock time?
items.back: Mirror time = 12:00 − time (use 11:60 − time when minutes ≠ 00). e.g. 3:25 → 8:35. Water image uses 6:00 base.
items.examPoint: Clock — mirror image of a given time

items.back: 5, 3, 1, 0. Ordinary year = 1 odd day, leap year = 2. Map total mod 7: 0=Sunday … 6=Saturday.
Divisible by 4, EXCEPT century years which must be divisible by 400. So 2000 leap; 1900 & 2100 not.
items.examPoint: Calendar — leap year rule (÷4, not ÷100 unless ÷400)

items.front: How much does a date advance to next year? When does a calendar repeat?
items.back: +1 day after an ordinary year, +2 after a leap year. Repeats when odd days ≡0 mod7 & leap-status matches (ordinary 6/11 yr, leap 28 yr).
items.examPoint: Calendar — repetition of a calendar (same-calendar year)

items.front: Method for ratio-of-ages problems over time?
items.back: Write parts as kx (5x, 7x); add/subtract the SAME time to each; equate to the new ratio and solve. Ratios are not preserved.
items.examPoint: Ages — present ages from a ratio plus a later condition
items.source: APPSC Quantitative Reasoning — Problem on Age

items.front: 'N years ago' and difference-based age relations?
items.back: Subtract N from BOTH ages before applying the relation ('hence' adds N). Age difference stays constant: if one is k older, A = B + k.
items.source: APPSC Quantitative Reasoning — Problem on Age

items.front: Added member's age from a change in average?
items.back: Added age = new_avg×(n+1) − old_avg×n; shortcut = new_avg + (rise × old count). e.g. 11 avg 29, +1 ⇒ coach = 41.
items.examPoint: Ages — average age (team/family, member added or replaced)
items.source: APPSC Quantitative Reasoning — Based on Cricket and Age
